question.text: Scenario: Ms. Prerna Desai, aged 28, is a software engineer earning Rs. 15 lakh per annum. She has the following financial goals: 1. Emergency fund: 6 months' expenses (monthly expenses Rs. 40,000) — needed immediately 2. Down payment for a house: Rs. 15 lakh in 3 years 3. Child's education fund: Rs. 50 lakh in 20 years 4. Retirement corpus: Rs. 5 crore in 32 years (retire at 60) She can save Rs. 50,000 per month. She is filing under the old tax regime and has not utilized her Section 80C limit. Her investment adviser, Mr. Kartik, suggests the following allocation: - Emergency fund: Rs. 2.4 lakh lump sum in a Liquid Fund (current yield ~6.5% p.a.) - House down payment: Rs. 30,000/month SIP in a Short Duration Debt Fund (expected return 7.5% p.a.) - Education fund: Rs. 10,000/month SIP in a Flexi-Cap Equity Fund (expected return 12% p.a., expense ratio 0.8% Direct Plan) - Retirement: Rs. 10,000/month SIP split between ELSS Fund (Rs. 5,000 for Section 80C) and Nifty 50 Index Fund (Rs. 5,000, expense ratio 0.15%) Total monthly SIP: Rs. 50,000. Prerna opts for Direct Plans and Growth option for all equity funds. Question 4 of 5: Mr. Kartik recommends Direct Plans for all of Prerna's investments. If the Flexi-Cap Fund has an expense ratio of 0.8% in Direct Plan versus 1.8% in Regular Plan, and both earn 12% gross return, what is the approximate difference in corpus after 20 years on a Rs. 10,000/month SIP (using end-of-month SIP and monthly net return = annual net return divided by 12)?

answer.text: Approximately Rs. 5-7 lakh more in Direct Plan
Approximately Rs. 11 lakh more in Direct Plan
Regular Plan will actually perform better

explanation.text: The Logic: Direct Plan net return is 12 percent - 0.8 percent = 11.2 percent per annum; Regular Plan net return is 12 percent - 1.8 percent = 10.2 percent per annum. On a Rs. 10,000 end-of-month SIP for 240 months, using monthly net return as the annual net return divided by 12, the Direct Plan corpus is about Rs. 88.9 lakh and the Regular Plan corpus is about Rs. 77.9 lakh, a difference of approximately Rs. 11 lakh. The Trap: A 1 percent annual expense difference looks small, but compounded over 20 years it produces a sizable gap in final corpus. Note: Direct Plans carry a lower expense ratio, which compounds into a higher net return over long horizons.
